The **rubab** ([UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_English "British English"): [/r ʊ ˈ b æ b/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"), [US](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_English "American English"): [/r ʊ ˈ b ɑː b/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")) or **robab**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-1) is a [lute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lute "Lute")-like musical instrument[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-Courtney-2) of [Central Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Asia "Central Asia") origin. It is the national musical instrument of [Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan "Afghanistan") and is also commonly played in [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") and [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"), mostly by [Balochis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baloch_people "Baloch people") and [Kashmiris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashmiri_people "Kashmiri people"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-3) and [Punjabis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punjabi_people "Punjabi people").

Variants of the rubab include the _Kabuli rebab_ of Afghanistan, the [Uyghur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs")_[rawap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rawap "Rawap")_ of [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang"), the _[Pamiri rubab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamiri\_rubab "Pamiri rubab")_ of [Tajikistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tajikistan "Tajikistan"), and the [North Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_India "North India")_[seni rebab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seni\_rebab "Seni rebab")_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-Vathsala2016-4) The instrument and its variants spread throughout West, Central, [South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Asia "South Asia") and [Southeast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia") Asia.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-Miner2004-5)

The Kabuli rebab from [Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan "Afghanistan")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-Courtney-2) derives its name from the [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic "Arabic")_[rebab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebab "Rebab")_ and is played with a [bow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bow_(music) "Bow (music)") while in Central Asia and the [Indian subcontinent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_subcontinent "Indian subcontinent"), the instrument is plucked and is distinctly different in construction.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-Vathsala2016-4)

## Construction

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Stamps_of_Azerbaijan%2C_2011-983.jpg/250px-Stamps_of_Azerbaijan%2C_2011-983.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Stamps_of_Azerbaijan,_2011-983.jpg)

2011 postal stamp of [Azerbaijan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azerbaijan "Azerbaijan") depicting a 19th-century rubab

The body is carved out of a single piece of wood, with a head covering a hollow bowl which provides the sound-chamber. The bridge sits on the skin and is held in position by the tension of the strings. It has three melody strings tuned in [fourths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_fourth "Perfect fourth"), two or three [drone strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_string "Drone string") and up to 15 [sympathetic strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sympathetic_strings "Sympathetic strings"). The instrument is made from the trunk of a [mulberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulberry "Mulberry") tree, the head from an animal skin such as goat, and the strings from the intestines of young goats (gut) or [nylon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nylon "Nylon").

## History

See also: [Lute §History and evolution of the lute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lute#History_and_evolution_of_the_lute "Lute"); and [History of lute-family instruments §Gambus and rabâb, skin tops plucked and bowed, rebab, rubab rabâb, robab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_lute-family_instruments#Gambus_and_rab%C3%A2b,_skin_tops_plucked_and_bowed,_rebab,_rubab_rab%C3%A2b,_robab "History of lute-family instruments")

The earliest historical record of an instrument named _rabab_ dates back to 10th-century Arabic texts, as identified by [Henry George Farmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_George_Farmer "Henry George Farmer"). This instrument, along with its variations like _rubab_, _rebab_, and _rabob_, subsequently gained popularity in various regions of West, Central, South, and Southeast Asia.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-6) It is mentioned in old [Persian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_literature "Persian literature") books, and many [Sufi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufi "Sufi") poets mention it in their poems. It is the traditional instrument of [Khorasan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Khorasan "Greater Khorasan") present Afghanistan and is widely used in countries such as [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"), [Azerbaijan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azerbaijan "Azerbaijan"), [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran"), [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"), [Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq "Iraq"), [Tajikistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tajikistan "Tajikistan"), and [Uzbekistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uzbekistan "Uzbekistan"), as well as in the [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang") province of northwest China and the [Jammu and Kashmir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jammu_and_Kashmir_(union_territory) "Jammu and Kashmir (union territory)") and [Punjab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punjab_(India) "Punjab (India)") regions of [northwest India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_India "North India").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-7)

The _rubab_ is known as "the lion of instruments" and is one of the two national instruments of Afghanistan (with the _[zerbaghali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zerbaghali "Zerbaghali")_).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-Vathsala2016-4) Classical Afghan music often features this instrument as a key component. Elsewhere it is known as the _Kabuli rebab_ in contrast to the _[Seni rebab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seni\_rebab "Seni rebab")_ of [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-Vathsala2016-4) In appearance, the Kabuli rubab looks slightly different from the Indian rubab.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-Kak1982-8) It is the ancestor of the north Indian _[sarod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarod "Sarod")_, although unlike the sarod, it is [fretted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fret "Fret").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-9)

The rubab was the first instrument used in [Sikhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikhism "Sikhism"); it was used by [Bhai Mardana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhai_Mardana "Bhai Mardana"), companion of the first guru, [Guru Nanak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guru_Nanak "Guru Nanak"). Whenever a [_shabad_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shabad_(hymn) "Shabad (hymn)") was revealed to Guru Nanak he would sing and Bhai Mardana would play on his rubab; he was known as a rababi. The rubab playing tradition is carried on by Sikhs such as [Namdharis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namdharis "Namdharis").

In 2024, [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO") recognised the art of creating the rubab as an [Intangible cultural heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intangible_cultural_heritage "Intangible cultural heritage") in Afghanistan, Iran, [Tajikistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tajikistan "Tajikistan") and [Uzbekistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uzbekistan "Uzbekistan").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-10)

## Variants

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/Photograph_of_rabab_players_%28rababis%29_titled_%27Lute_Players_Near_the_Golden_Temple%27%2C_taken_on_28_January_1903.jpg/250px-Photograph_of_rabab_players_%28rababis%29_titled_%27Lute_Players_Near_the_Golden_Temple%27%2C_taken_on_28_January_1903.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Photograph_of_rabab_players_(rababis)_titled_'Lute_Players_Near_the_Golden_Temple',_taken_on_28_January_1903.jpg)

Photograph of rabab players ([rababis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rababi "Rababi")) titled 'Lute Players Near the [Golden Temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Temple "Golden Temple")', taken on 28 January 1903

In [northern India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_India "Northern India"), the [seni rebab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seni_rebab "Seni rebab"), which emerged during the [Mughal Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_Empire "Mughal Empire"), has "a large hook at the back of its head, making it easier for a musician to sling it over the shoulder and play it even while walking."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-Vathsala2016-4)

The [Sikh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikh_Empire "Sikh Empire") rabab was traditionally a local Punjabi variant known as the 'Firandia' rabab ([Punjabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punjabi_language "Punjabi language"): ਫਿਰੰਦੀਆ ਰਬਾਬ _Phiradī'ā rabāba_),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-14) however Baldeep Singh, an expert in the Sikh musical tradition, challenges this narrative.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-16)

In Tajikistan a similar but somewhat distinct _rubab-i-pamir_ ([Pamiri rubab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamiri_rubab "Pamiri rubab")) is played, employing a shallower body and neck.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-17) The _rubab_ of the [Pamir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pamir "Great Pamir") area has six gut strings, one of which, rather than running from the head to the bridge, is attached partway down the neck, similar to the fifth string of the American [banjo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banjo "Banjo").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubab_(instrument)#cite_note-18)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

For the company, see [National Instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Instruments "National Instruments").

This list contains [musical instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_instrument "Musical instrument") of symbolic or cultural importance within a [nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nation "Nation"), [state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_state "Sovereign state"), [ethnicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnicity "Ethnicity"), [tribe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribe "Tribe") or other group of people.

In some cases, national instruments remain in wide use within the nation (such as the [Puerto Rican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico")_[cuatro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuatro\_(instrument) "Cuatro (instrument)")_), but in others, their importance is primarily symbolic (such as the Welsh triple harp). Danish ethnologist Lisbet Torp has concluded that some national instrument traditions, such as the [Finnish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_people "Finnish people")_[kantele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kantele "Kantele")_, are invented, pointing to the "influence of intellectuals and nationalists in the nationwide promotion of selected musical instruments as a vehicle for [nationalistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalism "Nationalism") ideas".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_instruments_(music)#cite_note-NI-1) Governments do not generally officially recognize national instruments; some exceptions being the [Paraguayan harp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguayan_harp "Paraguayan harp"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_instruments_(music)#cite_note-2) the [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_people "Japanese people")_[koto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koto\_(musical\_instrument) "Koto (musical instrument)")_[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_instruments_(music)#cite_note-3) and the [Trinidadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinidad "Trinidad")[steelpan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steelpan "Steelpan").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_instruments_(music)#cite_note-steelpan-4)

This list compiles instruments that have been alleged to be a _national instrument_ by any of a variety of sources, and an instrument's presence on the list does not indicate that its status as a national instrument is indisputable, only that its status has been credibly argued. Each instrument on this list has a [Hornbostel-Sachs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hornbostel-Sachs "Hornbostel-Sachs") number immediately below it. This number indicates the instrument's classification within the Hornbostel-Sachs system (H-S), which organizes instruments numerically based on the manner in which they produce sound.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_instruments_(music)#cite_note-5)

Images and recordings are supplied where available; note that there are often variations within a national musical tradition, and thus the images and recordings may not be accurate in depicting the entire spectrum of the given nation's music, and that some images and recordings may be taken from a region outside the core of the national instrument's home when such distinctions have little relevance to the information present in the image and recordings. A number of countries have more than one instrument listed, each having been described as a _national instrument_, not usually by the same source; neither the presence of multiple entries for one nation, nor for multiple nations for one instrument, on this list is reflective of active dispute in any instance. Alternative names and spellings are given. These mostly come from alternative spellings within English or alternative methods of [transliterating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transliteration "Transliteration") from a foreign language to English, such as the [Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_people "Chinese people")_[yangqin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangqin "Yangqin")_, also transliterated _yang ch'in_ and _yang qin_. Others reflect regions or subcultures within a given nation, such as the Australian [didgeridoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didgeridoo "Didgeridoo") which is or has been called _didjeridu_, _yidaki_, _yiraki_, _magu_, _kanbi_ and _ihambilbilg_ in various [Australian Aboriginal languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Aboriginal_languages "Australian Aboriginal languages").
